standard.title: Read using phonic knowledge
standard.description: read decodable and authentic texts using developing phonic knowledge, and monitor meaning using context and emerging grammatical knowledge
standard.prior_knowledge: Students are developing letter-sound knowledge (AC9EFLY11, AC9EFLY12). They have not yet been asked to apply phonic decoding strategies within connected text, or to monitor for meaning breakdown and self-correct using context.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can read decodable and authentic texts using developing phonic knowledge — navigating correctly, attempting unknown words using phonics, and monitoring for meaning using context and grammatical knowledge.

nodes.label: Navigate a text correctly
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can navigate a text from left to right, top to bottom, matching one spoken word to one written word.
nodes.minimum_width: Read a short familiar text pointing to each word, maintaining left-to-right directionality and one-to-one word matching.
nodes.typical_width: Navigate a text correctly — starting at the right place, reading left to right and top to bottom, returning to the next line correctly, matching one spoken word to one written word.
wider: Apply navigation skills across a range of text formats — big books, small books, and simple digital texts
Read familiar texts at varying speeds while maintaining accurate tracking and word matching
nodes.hinge_reason: Without accurate directional tracking and one-to-one word matching, phonic decoding in Node 2 cannot function — students cannot attempt to decode a word they have not correctly isolated on the page.

response_modes.reason: Accurate tracking and one-to-one word matching must become automatic — they are the foundation of all reading. Practice across multiple texts builds the habit. Errors (losing track, skipping lines) cascade into comprehension breakdown.

success_criteria: Student tracks from left to right consistently across a full page of text.
Student correctly matches each spoken word to one written word.
Student returns correctly to the start of the next line.

nodes.label: Use phonic knowledge to decode
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can attempt to decode unknown words using their developing letter-sound knowledge and high-frequency word knowledge.
nodes.minimum_width: Attempt at least one unknown word in a familiar text using letter-sound decoding.
nodes.typical_width: Attempt to work out unknown words using phonic decoding and knowledge of high-frequency words; blend sounds to decode CVC and simple words encountered in text.
wider: Apply decoding strategies to an increasing range of text types — decodable readers, picture books, simple information texts
Apply phonic decoding to names and topic words from culturally diverse contexts in classroom texts
Use multiple decoding strategies (phonics, word recognition, context) and explain which strategy was used
nodes.hinge_reason: Decoding is the prerequisite for meaning monitoring in Node 3 — students cannot notice that their reading does not make sense if they are not producing an approximation of the word through phonic attempt. Without decoding, self-correction has no raw material to work with.

response_modes.reason: Students may apply phonics only in isolated word tasks and not carry the strategy into connected text. Multiple connected text contexts — including authentic texts not just decodables — help generalise the strategy.

success_criteria: Student attempts an unknown word using phonics rather than guessing randomly.
Student can blend sounds to produce a recognisable word in at least one attempt.

nodes.label: Monitor meaning and self-correct
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise when their reading does not make sense and pause or seek support — using context and emerging grammatical knowledge as a check.
nodes.minimum_width: Pause when reading breaks down and attempt to self-correct or seek support.
nodes.typical_width: Monitor meaning while reading — pause or ask for support when something does not make sense; use context (what would make sense here?) and emerging grammatical knowledge (does that sound right?) alongside phonics to monitor and repair.
wider: Apply monitoring strategies across texts of increasing length and complexity
Explicitly articulate what strategy was used when meaning broke down — identifying the source of difficulty
Apply monitoring strategies to texts with culturally unfamiliar content, using context more heavily when phonics alone is insufficient

response_modes.reason: Monitoring meaning requires integrating multiple cueing systems simultaneously — phonics, context and grammar — rather than relying on one. Coordinating these is the endpoint of Foundation-level reading.

success_criteria: Student notices when their reading does not make sense.
Student pauses or attempts to self-correct without needing a prompt.
Student can say what they tried when meaning broke down.
